title: Inquest begins into RCMP shooting of teen
article: Sixteen-year-old Kyle Tait was sitting in the passenger seat of a stolen SUV when he was shot to death by a British Columbia police officer.
Was the officer too quick to use his gun? Or was a fellow officer's life in danger?
A coroner's jury will attempt to find the truth in an inquest starting today into the police-shooting death of Mr. Tait, from Surrey.
Mr. Tait's family claims in a lawsuit that Constable Todd Sweet approached the vehicle "agitated and enraged" after a police chase, "and fired several bullets indiscriminately into the vehicle."

The New Westminster Police version of the shooting is much different. "The suspect vehicle rammed the police vehicle in the area of the passenger side," says an August, 2005, news release sent out two days after the shooting. "The passenger officer was now trapped in the police vehicle."
Police said the officer who was driving the vehicle fired three rounds from his weapon when the driver of the stolen vehicle failed to stop.
One of those bullets hit the driver in the hand while a second bullet killed Mr. Tait.
Constable Sweet, who has been on paid suspension for about a year for an incident unrelated to the shooting, wasn't charged in relation to Mr. Tait's death.
"There has been no criminal finding," said Sergeant Ivan Chu of the New Westminster Police department.
Sgt. Chu said the suspension came after a second allegation that Constable Sweet kicked a suspect in the head while the man was handcuffed on the ground.
Constable Sweet admitted to assault in court last July and was given a suspended sentence.
Sgt. Chu said founded allegations are dealt with quickly by the department.
"Anybody can make an allegation of a police officer," Sgt. Chu added. "Constable Sweet happened to be a very out-there type patrol officer, where he's dealing with a certain element of the public."
The coroner's inquest, which will last about eight days, is not meant to find fault.
The inquest is considered a fact-finding investigation and may not make any findings of legal responsibility.
When Constable Sweet fired into the 1996 GMC Yukon, there were five teenagers inside.
Officers had pulled the vehicle over early that morning, but the 18-year-old driver then sped off when the officer walked to the driver's side door.
The driver, Ian Campbell, was convicted of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle, possession of stolen property and operating a vehicle in police pursuit.
A charge of criminal negligence causing Mr. Tait's death was stayed by the court.
Mr. Tait's mother, Noel, and his stepfather, Kevin Webb, dispute the police version of the events in a wrongful-death lawsuit filed in B.C. Supreme Court.
"At the time of the shooting, the vehicle's engine was not running and the five occupants were unarmed," the lawsuit states.
"None of the occupants of the vehicle, including Kyle Tait, posed any risk of harm to the defendant Sweet or others."
A second damage lawsuit has been filed against Constable Sweet and the City of New Westminster in connection to the assault case.
Anthony White, the victim in that case, claims the city knew of the officer's aggressive reputation but failed to take action.

Sgt. Chu explained that once the inquest is complete, a Police Act investigation will be finished surrounding the shooting to determine what, if any, disciplinary action will be taken against Constable Sweet.
Sgt. Chu said sanctions could range from a verbal reprimand to termination.
An officer of the New Westminster Police shot Kyle Tait in 2005. The RCMP was incorrectly named in a headline in yesterday's newspaper.
